A run is **unfinished** at stage $j$ if it has not entered a stopping subspace by $t_j$; otherwise it is **stopped**. The stopping subspaces are pairwise orthogonal, and the output register labels each stopped branch as **good** or **bad**. Every later stage is controlled on the unfinished projector, so a stopped branch is not advanced. The input specifies each stage unitary, its inverse and every controlled form used, and the gate/query cost for each.

$$T_{\rm av}:=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i t_i^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Let $p_{\rm succ}$ be the total Born probability of the good-output subspace. When $p_{\rm succ}>0$, the good output means the normalized conditional state of the declared good projector; it is defined only on that positive-probability branch. for every basis input $x$ and every target string $y$. It uses at most $6S+4E+m$ elementary gate occurrences, at most $S+E$ clean work bits, and serial depth at most $6S+4E+m$. The same operator action holds coherently on arbitrary superpositions and after adjoining any finite reference register.

derivations.claim: Put $a=\arctan(1/5)$ and $b=\arctan(1/239)$. Principal monotonicity and $\tan(\pi/4)=1$ give $0<b<a<\pi/4$. The tangent double-angle formula gives $\tan(2a)=5/12<1$, so $2a<\pi/4$ and $0<4a<\pi/2$. A second doubling gives $\tan(4a)=120/119>1$, hence $4a>\pi/4>b$. The subtraction formula gives $$\tan(4a-b)=\frac{120/119-1/239}{1+(120/119)(1/239)}=1.$$ All denominators are positive, and $0<4a-b<4a<\pi/2$. Injectivity of the principal tangent branch therefore proves $4a-b=\pi/4$, or $\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$. This is a local proof of the needed Machin identity. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

For $0\le x<1$ and any integer $J\ge1$, the exact finite geometric identity is $$\frac1{1+t^2}=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}(-1)^jt^{2j} +\frac{(-1)^Jt^{2J}}{1+t^2}.$$ Integrating from zero to $x$ and using the arctangent integral yields $$\left|\arctan x-\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\frac{(-1)^jx^{2j+1}}{2j+1}\right| \le\frac{x^{2J+1}}{2J+1}.$$ This is a finite bound, requiring no limit test during the algorithm. Set $J=k+8$ and form the exact rational $$\widehat\pi=16\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(2j+1)5^{2j+1}} -4\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(2j+1)239^{2j+1}}.$$ Steps 1.1–1.2 give $$|\widehat\pi-\pi|\le\frac{20}{5^{2J+1}} \le\frac1{1024M^2},$$ because $5^{2k}\ge2^{2k}=M^2$ and $20\cdot1024<5^{17}$. In particular $0<\widehat\pi<4$: for the lower bound, $\pi/4=\int_0^1(1+t^2)^{-1}\,dt>1/2$ gives $\pi>2$; for the upper bound, step 1.1 and $\arctan(1/5)<1/5$ give $\pi<16/5$, and the displayed error is below $1/1024$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

Set $x=\widehat\pi y/M$, so $0\le x<4$, and set the even integer $n=16(k+4)$. Compute the exact rational sine polynomial $$S(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n/2-1}\frac{(-1)^jx^{2j+1}}{(2j+1)!}.$$ Every derivative of sine has absolute value at most one. The Taylor remainder bound at degree $n-1$ gives $$|S(x)-\sin x|\le\frac{4^n}{n!} \le\left(\frac{32}{n}\right)^{n/2} \le2^{-n/2}\le\frac1{4096M^2}.$$ Indeed the last $n/2$ factors in $n!$ are at least $n/2$, so $n!\ge(n/2)^{n/2}$, and $n\ge96\ge64$. Finally $n/2=8(k+4)\ge2k+12$ gives the stated precision. [F3, F4, algebra]

The derivative bound for sine and the mean value theorem give $|\sin x-\sin(\pi y/M)|\le|\widehat\pi-\pi|y/M \le1/(1024M^2)$. Put $s=\sin(\pi y/M)$ and $d=5/(4096M^2)$. Step 2.1 implies $|S(x)-s|\le d<1$ and $|s|\le1$. Consequently $$|S(x)^2-s^2|\le d(2+d)\le3d =\frac{15}{4096M^2}<\frac1{4M^2}.$$ Thus the exact rational square $r=S(x)^2$ approximates the desired probability with absolute error strictly below $1/(4M^2)$. [F3, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

If $y=0$, set $a_M(y)=0$ explicitly. Otherwise write the exact rational $r=U/V$ with integers $U\ge0$ and $V>0$, without requiring cancellation to lowest terms. Use integer division to compute $$q=\left\lfloor\frac{2M^2U+V}{2V}\right\rfloor,\qquad a_M(y)=\min(M^2,\max(0,q)).$$ The floor rule is deterministic nearest-grid rounding, breaking rational half-grid ties upward. Hence $|q/M^2-r|\le1/(2M^2)$. Clipping to $[0,1]$ cannot increase distance from the true probability $s^2\in[0,1]$. Step 2.2 therefore gives $$\left|a_M(y)/M^2-s^2\right| <\frac1{4M^2}+\frac1{2M^2}=\frac3{4M^2}.$$ For $y=0$, the exact target is zero, so the bound also holds. Every comparison in this procedure compares finite integers, including any tie; there is no comparison against an exact transcendental number. [given, step 2.2, algebra]

All rational computations above have polynomial bit length in $k$. For the arctangent sum at $q\in\{5,239\}$, one may take as an unreduced common denominator $D_q=\prod_{j=0}^{J-1}(2j+1)q^{2j+1}$, whose bit length is $O(J^2+J\log(J+1))=O(k^2)$. Obtain each numerator by exact division of this known multiple, then sum with the indicated signs. A common denominator for $\widehat\pi$ is $D_5D_{239}$, still of $O(k^2)$ bits; the same bound holds for its numerator. Therefore $x=P/Q$ can be written with integer $P\ge0$, $Q>0$ of $O(k^2)$ bits, without rational reduction. [step 1.2, algebra]

A common denominator for the sine polynomial is $D=Q^{n-1}(n-1)!$. Its $j$th integer numerator term is $$(-1)^jP^{2j+1}Q^{n-2j-2}\frac{(n-1)!}{(2j+1)!}.$$ All exponents are nonnegative and every indicated division is exact. The powers, factorials, terms, common denominator, and signed partial sums have $O(k^3)$ bits: $n=O(k)$, $\log P,\log Q=O(k^2)$, and $\log((n-1)!)=O(k\log(k+1))$. Summing $O(k)$ terms adds only $O(\log(k+1))$ extra bits. Thus $S=A/D$ can be computed with $O(k^3)$-bit signed integers; $U=A^2$, $V=D^2$, and the final integer division in step 3.1 have the same bit-length order. [step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

There are only polynomially many arithmetic operations: products for the two denominators, powers and factorials, $O(k)$ Taylor terms and their exact divisions, and one final quotient/clamp. Schoolbook addition, subtraction and comparison of $L$-bit integers use $O(L)$ elementary Boolean operations, multiplication uses $O(L^2)$ operations by summing shifted partial products, and long division uses $O(L^2)$ operations by $O(L)$ shift/compare/subtract stages. Signed integers can use a sign bit and a magnitude of the fixed safe length; all denominators are known positive. The operation counts and safe register lengths depend only on $k$. Unroll their loops and implement data branches by Boolean selection between the two computed results. Thus a deterministic classical generator produces a Boolean DAG for $y\mapsto a_M(y)$ of polynomial size and description length in $k$, in polynomial time. This also covers generation of the rational constants; no constant table of exponential length or unit-cost unbounded integer arithmetic is assumed. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, construct, algebra]

Apply compute-copy-reverse to that Boolean DAG: evaluate its nodes in fresh clean bits, XOR-copy its $(2k+1)$ output bits to $z$, and reverse every evaluation gate. The inspected reversible embedding theorem gives the asserted XOR action, polynomial elementary gate count, serial depth and clean workspace, all restored to zero. The Boolean circuit's uniform generation proof in step 4.3, followed by the finite node-gadget compiler, gives polynomial-time generation of the actual reversible gate list. The clean identity extends by linearity to coherent inputs and finite references. Its actual reversal has identical gate count. For an external control, either use a compute/controlled-copy/uncompute construction on the same Boolean function, or control the fixed reversible gate list; the former directly gives a constant-factor resource increase and restores all scratch. No real-number refinement or measurement occurs. This proves the Statement. [F6, step 4.3, construct, algebra] ∎

**Rounding mode.** Select `exact-cyclotomic` (the original finite comparison mode below) or `efficient-grid`. In `efficient-grid` mode replace only RoundedAE output rounding: run [[lem-qa-coherent-amplitude-grid-rounding]] on the measured $k$-bit label $y$, with $M=2^k$, and return $a_M(y)/M^2$. Its range is $[0,1]$, zero label returns zero, and absolute error is at most $3/(4M^2)<M^{-2}$. All following thresholds, medians, caps and scale choices are unchanged. The helper supplies actual uniform polynomial-in-$\log M$ generation, elementary reversible gates and work, with actual inverse/control versions; use those costs in this mode.

**Input.** An arbitrary finite-dimensional amplitude-estimation instance from [[def-qa-13-amplitude-estimation-task]], with unitary sampler $A$, initial vector $|0\rangle$, supplied orthogonal success projection $\Pi$, and unknown probability $p=\|\Pi A|0\rangle\|^2$; rational parameters $0<p_{\min}\le1$, $0<c<1/4$, and $0<\beta<1$; and the promise $p=0$ or $p\ge p_{\min}$.

Use the repeated controlled-unitary access mode with $Q=-AS_0A^*S_{\rm good}$ from that task definition. Controlled $A$, controlled $A^*$, controlled $S_0$, controlled $S_{\rm good}$, and the control phase are explicitly supplied or implemented with declared costs. An ordinary preparation $A|0\rangle$ is also available and charged. Ordinary uncontrolled sampler access alone does not supply these controlled capabilities.

**Output.** A rational estimate $\widehat p\in[0,1]$. The procedure uses independent fresh estimator workspaces, measures and discards them, and returns only classical data. Any subsequent use of a sampler starts a fresh execution from its declared initial vector.

**Instructions.** Set $M_j=4\cdot2^j$. Determine the least integer $L\ge0$ with $M_L^2p_{\min}\ge1024$ by doubling and rational comparison. Set $\delta=\min\{1/16,\beta/(L+2)\}$. Choose the least positive odd integer $r$ with $(4/5)^r\le\delta$, using rational multiplication and comparison.

For each dyadic integer $M\ge4$, define the following two subprocedures.

1. $\operatorname{RoundedAE}(M)$ runs [[alg-qa-13-phase-estimation-amplitude-estimation]] with label size $M$, obtaining the exact real cyclotomic output $z=\sin^2(\pi y/M)$. If $y=0$, return zero. Otherwise use [[lem-qa-13-real-cyclotomic-comparison]] and binary search among the integers $0\le t\le M^2$ to find the largest $t$ with $t/M^2\le z$, and return $t/M^2$. Equality is decided by the same exact comparison procedure; $z=1$ returns $1$.
2. $\operatorname{MedAE}(M)$ runs $r$ independent copies of $\operatorname{RoundedAE}(M)$ and returns their middle order statistic, using rational comparisons.

For $j=0,\ldots,L$ in order, compute $b_j=\operatorname{MedAE}(M_j)$. If $b_j\ge256/M_j^2$, stop this loop at $J=j$, choose the least power of two $N\ge16M_J/c$, and return the output of a fresh $\operatorname{MedAE}(N)$. If no such detection occurs through $j=L$, return zero without a final estimation call.

Query, preparation, ordinary-gate, measurement and classical-bit costs are separate coordinates. All exact comparisons, cyclotomic encoding, rational arithmetic, sorting, and output writing are charged as classical bit operations under [[def-qa-classical-bit-cost]]. The comparison supplier asserts termination, without a polynomial bit-cost bound.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $|0\rangle$ a specified unit vector, $A:H\to H$ a supplied unitary, and $\Pi_{\rm good}$ an explicitly supplied orthogonal projection. Put
$$S_0=I-2|0\rangle\langle0|,\qquad S_{\rm good}=I-2\Pi_{\rm good},\qquad Q=-A S_0A^*S_{\rm good}.$$
Each classical instance has an injective encoding $\operatorname{enc}$ from its declared instance set into $\{0,1\}^*$, with input size $|\operatorname{enc}(z)|$; the promise domain and output obligation are stated for that task. Supplied operator or oracle access is a separate resource declaration.

The success amplitude is $a=\|\Pi_{\rm good}A|0\rangle\|^2\in[0,1]$, and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt a\in[0,\pi/2]$. Amplitude estimation returns an algebraically encoded estimate of $a$; its requested accuracy and failure probability are stated separately.

For counting, let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and set $N=2^n$ with address basis $\{|x\rangle:x\in\{0,1\}^n\}$ and a Boolean predicate $f$. Set $A=H^{\otimes n}$, $|0\rangle=|0^n\rangle$, $\Pi_{\rm good}=\sum_{f(x)=1}|x\rangle\langle x|$, and $t=|\{x:f(x)=1\}|$. Then the counting amplitude is $a=t/N$. The preparation uses exactly $n$ ordinary Hadamard gates. Access to the controlled membership reflection is a separate explicit resource.

Two phase-estimation access modes are allowed. In the power-query mode, the model supplies each $C(Q^{2^j})$ for $0\le j<m$ as one declared query, with its individual cost recorded. In the repeated-unitary mode the model supplies $C(Q)$ and implements $C(Q^{2^j})$ by $2^j$ sequential calls, for exactly $2^m-1$ controlled-$Q$ calls. In repeated-unitary mode, each controlled-$Q$ call expands as the composite $C(-I)C(A)C(S_0)C(A^*)C(S_{\rm good})$; controlled $A$, controlled $A^*$, controlled $S_0$, controlled $S_{\rm good}$, and the control phase $C(-I)$ must all be supplied or implemented and charged. In power-query mode each supplied controlled power has its own declared cost vector, including any constituent implementations the model uses. An uncontrolled phase query does not supply any of them. Query, ordinary-gate, state-preparation, measurement, and classical bit costs are separate coordinates.

**Input.** An instance from [[def-qa-13-amplitude-estimation-task]], an integer $m\ge2$, $M=2^m$, and either the declared controlled-power access mode or repeated controlled-$Q$ access.

**Instructions.** Prepare $\psi=A|0\rangle$, run the $M$-label QPE circuit on $Q$ using controlled powers $Q^{2^j}$, $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, and measure its phase register to obtain $y\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$. Output the exact cyclotomic value
$$\widetilde a=\sin^2(\pi y/M)=\frac{2-\zeta_M^y-\zeta_M^{-y}}4,\qquad \zeta_M=e^{2\pi i/M},$$
with the real embedding specified by this root. A decimal approximation is postprocessing and is charged separately. The leading minus in $Q$ is retained: on a controlled call it is the control phase $C(-I)$, not a discarded standalone global phase.

For the QFT-based estimator with $M=2^m\ge4$ and integer $k\ge1$, its output satisfies
$$|\widetilde a-a|\le\frac{2\pi k\sqrt{a(1-a)}}M+\frac{\pi^2k^2}{M^2}$$
with probability at least $8/\pi^2$ when $k=1$, and with probability strictly greater than $1-1/[2(k-1)]$ when $k\ge2$. In particular the $k=1$ error is at most $\pi/M+\pi^2/M^2$. At $a=0$ the output is exactly zero; at $a=1$ it is exactly one.
The circle constant satisfies $3<\pi<22/7$.

For $M=2^m\ge4$, repeated controlled-$Q$ access uses exactly $M-1$ controlled-$Q$ applications in one run; each expands to one call each to controlled $A$, controlled $A^*$, controlled $S_0$, controlled $S_{\rm good}$, and the control phase. Supplied controlled-power access uses exactly $m$ power queries and reports their separate costs. With fixed success probability, additive amplitude error $\epsilon\in(0,1]$ is obtained with $M=\Theta(1/\epsilon)$, hence $O(1/\epsilon)$ repeated controlled-$Q$ calls; state preparation, ordinary gates, and classical encoding are separate costs.

For an integer $s\ge2$, let $\zeta_s=e^{2\pi i/s}$ and let $P,R\in\mathbb Q[X]$ be given coefficient lists such that $P(\zeta_s)$ and $R(\zeta_s)$ are real. There is a terminating deterministic exact procedure to decide which of these two real numbers is larger, or whether they are equal. Its bit-operation cost is charged to the classical cost model; no polynomial bound is asserted.

For a classical query algorithm [[def-qa-classical-query-algorithm]], bit-operation cost is the number of transitions of a declared multitape Turing machine over a fixed finite alphabet; the $k$-tape transition reads and writes one symbol on each of its $k\ge1$ tapes and moves each head once per transition ([[def-multitape-and-nondeterministic-machines]]). It includes random-bit generation, input-encoding work [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]], address formation, reading and writing every bit of an oracle reply, comparison/postprocessing, and writing the classical output. The fair-bit machine convention is supplied by [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The oracle invocation itself is one separately counted query action; its returned bits are not free to process.

For a query with an $a(n)$-bit address and a $b(n)$-bit reply, the machine's charged work includes forming the address and processing the $b(n)$ reply symbols. A claimed time bound also specifies whether it is worst-case over promised inputs and random tapes, as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. Query, nonoracle quantum gate, measurement, and classical bit costs remain distinct.

For every integer $k\ge2$, put $M=2^k$. There is a deterministic uniformly
generated finite reversible circuit with the action

$$|y,z,0^w\rangle\longmapsto|y,z\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}a_M(y),0^w\rangle$$

for every $k$-bit integer $0\le y<M$ and every $(2k+1)$-bit target $z$,
where $a_M(y)$ is an integer satisfying

$$0\le a_M(y)\le M^2,\qquad a_M(0)=0,\qquad
\left|\frac{a_M(y)}{M^2}-\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi y}{M}\right)\right|
\le\frac{3}{4M^2}.$$

Circuit generation time, gate count in $X$, CNOT and Toffoli, serial depth,
and clean workspace are all polynomial in $k$. The identity holds on
arbitrary coherent inputs and with finite reference registers. Its actual
inverse and coherent controls have the same polynomial resource order.
The algorithm uses only bounded exact integer/rational arithmetic with
fixed loop counts depending on $k$; it performs no real equality test or
equality-dependent precision refinement. The output encodes the rational
$a_M(y)/M^2$ by its numerator and the known fixed denominator.

derivations.claim: The dyadic sequence $M_j=4\cdot2^j$ has unbounded squares, so its positive rational threshold in [F1] is eventually reached. Since $p_{\min}\le1$, its least cap index has $L\ge3$, and minimality gives $M_{L-1}^2p_{\min}<1024$, hence $M_L<64/\sqrt{p_{\min}}$. The geometric sequence $(4/5)^r$ tends to zero, so the least positive odd $r$ in [F1] exists. The final scale is a finite dyadic ceiling of a rational number and satisfies $16M_J/c\le N<32M_J/c$. Every raw call has dyadic size at least four. Thus all schedule choices are executable by finite rational arithmetic. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

For each raw output $z\in[0,1]$, the rounding instruction finds $t=\lfloor M^2z\rfloor$ by finite binary search with [F7], including equality and the endpoint $z=1$. Its returned rational $b=t/M^2$ satisfies $0\le z-b<M^{-2}$, with equality $b=z$ when $M^2z$ is integral, and returns exactly zero when $y=0$. Binary search uses $O(\log M)$ comparisons. Its rational output has $O(\log M)$ numerator and denominator bits. Every comparison terminates by [F7], and all its internal refinement and output operations remain charged under [F8]. In efficient-grid mode [F9] supplies the same range, zero branch and $M^{-2}$ error directly, with its separately proved finite polynomial resource bound; no exact-comparison refinement is used in that mode. There are at most $L+1$ detection medians and one final median, each with finitely many calls, so the entire procedure terminates. [F1, F3, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

By [F5], $8/\pi^2>8/(22/7)^2>4/5$, $2\pi<8$, and $\pi^2<16$. Therefore [F4] and step 1.2 imply that each rounded output lies in the interval $I_M=[p-8\sqrt p/M-17/M^2,p+8\sqrt p/M+17/M^2]$ with failure probability at most $1/5$. Let $B_i$ indicate failure of copy $i$ in a median, and put $B=\sum_{i=1}^rB_i$. Independence gives $\mathbb E4^B=\prod_i\mathbb E4^{B_i}\le(8/5)^r$. Since $\mathbf1_{\{B\ge r/2\}}\le4^B/4^{r/2}$, taking expectations gives $\Pr\{B\ge r/2\}\le(4/5)^r\le\delta$. If fewer than half of the samples miss $I_M$, their middle order statistic lies in $I_M$: an order statistic outside that interval would put at least $(r+1)/2$ samples on the same outside side. Consequently each median misses $I_M$ with probability at most $\delta$. This also holds conditional on every earlier classical transcript, because the chosen size is then fixed and this median uses independent fresh workspaces. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

Call a median good when it belongs to $I_M$, and put $x=M\sqrt p$. At a good detection stage, $x^2-8x-17\le M^2b\le x^2+8x+17$. A good stage that detects therefore has $x>11$, since for $0\le x\le11$ its upper bound is at most $121+88+17=226<256$. A good stage with $x\ge32$ certainly detects, since $x^2-8x-17$ is increasing there and is at least $751>256$. For a positive promised $p$, $M_L\sqrt p\ge32$, so a good cap stage detects. [given, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

If detection occurs at a good stage $J$, then the fresh final scale has $x'=N\sqrt p\ge16M_J\sqrt p/c>176/c$. When its final median is good, $|\widehat p-p|/p\le8/x'+17/(x')^2<c/22+17c^2/176^2<c$, using $0<c<1/4$. At most $L+2$ medians are invoked, and each has conditional failure probability at most $\delta$ by step 2.1. The union bound therefore makes the probability of any invoked bad median at most $(L+2)\delta\le\beta$. On the complementary event, a positive input detects by the cap and satisfies the relative estimate just proved. At $p=0$, [F4] gives raw output zero with certainty; step 1.2 and the algorithm's zero-label branch make every rounded value and median zero. No positive threshold is met, so the algorithm returns zero exactly. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

By [F6], one rounded call at size $M$ uses $M-1$ controlled $A$ calls, $M-1$ controlled $A^*$ calls and one ordinary $A$ preparation, for $2M-1$ sampler-and-inverse invocations. A median costs at most $2rM$ such invocations, with separately charged $r(M-1)$ occurrences of each controlled reflection and control phase. Since $\sum_{j=0}^LM_j<2M_L$, detection costs less than $4rM_L$. A final median, if invoked, has size $N<32M_L/c$ and costs less than $64rM_L/c$. Thus every execution, including unsuccessful estimates reaching the cap, has $C<4rM_L+64rM_L/c<65rM_L/c<4160r/(c\sqrt{p_{\min}})$, because $4c<1$. [given, F1, F2, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

Suppose $p>0$. Let $j_*$ be the first index with $M_{j_*}\sqrt p\ge32$. It exists by the promise and satisfies $j_*\le L$, $j_*>0$, and $M_{j_*}<64/\sqrt p$. For analysis, preassign independent hypothetical median outcomes to all detection stages, and reveal them only if reached; this finite product of independent experiments has exactly the procedure's law. To reach stage $j_*+t\le L$, every one of the $t$ preceding stages beginning at $j_*$ must have a bad median, since a good one at these scales would detect by step 2.2. Thus $\Pr\{\text{reach }j_*+t\}\le\delta^t$. If $S$ is the sum of sizes of invoked detection stages, finite summation and $\delta\le1/16$ give $\mathbb ES<2M_{j_*}+M_{j_*}\sum_{t\ge1}(2\delta)^t\le(2+1/7)M_{j_*}<3M_{j_*}$. The infinite geometric sum here is only an upper bound on a finite expected cost. [given, F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

Detection costs at most $2rS$. If detection occurs, $M_J\le S$ and the final median costs less than $64rM_J/c$; otherwise that cost is zero. Hence $\mathbb EC\le(2+64/c)r\mathbb ES<200rM_{j_*}/c<12800r/(c\sqrt p)$. If $p=0$, there is no final median and $C<4rM_L<256r/\sqrt{p_{\min}}$. Both cases imply $\mathbb EC=O(r/(c\sqrt{p_*}))$. On the probability-$1-\beta$ event of step 2.3, a positive input stops by $j_*$, so the deterministic calculation of step 3.1, with $M_{j_*}$ replacing $M_L$, gives $C<65rM_{j_*}/c<4160r/(c\sqrt p)$. For $p=0$ the deterministic cap already gives the claimed $p_*$ bound. This establishes the simultaneous probability assertion. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

Minimal dyadic threshold choice gives $L=O(1+\log(1/p_{\min}))$. Since $r$ is the least positive odd integer with $(4/5)^r\le\delta$, it is at most two above the real threshold $\log(1/\delta)/\log(5/4)$, apart from the harmless minimum value one. Also $1/\delta=\max\{16,(L+2)/\beta\}$, so $r=O(1+\log((L+2)/\beta))$. Substituting into step 3.3 gives the stated expected bound. Rounding's precision and finite comparison count are those of step 1.2, and [F8] keeps their actual bit costs, along with the ordinary quantum resources in [F6], separate from this query bound. Finally, by [F1] every measured estimation workspace is discarded and the output is classical. Conditional on any resulting transcript, a subsequent fresh execution initializes its own declared input and applies its own prescribed sampler. Its output state, and therefore its conditional good state when that event has positive probability, is precisely that prescribed for the fresh sampler; the measured construction registers are not inputs to it. [given, F1, F6, F8, step 1.2, step 3.3, algebra] ∎

Input a finite-register coherent preparation $U$ with good projection $P$, as in [[def-qa-12-prepared-success-subspace]], and represented rational parameters $0<p_0\le1$ and $0<\beta<1$. The success promise is $p:=\|PU|0\rangle\|^2\ge p_0$. Supply $U^\dagger$ under [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]], the reflections $S_0=I-2|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $S_g=I-2P$ under [[def-qc-reflection]], and the controlled versions of all operations used under [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. The good/bad instrument is the projective measurement $\{P,I-P\}$ of [[def-qc-projective-measurement]]. It may be supplied directly or implemented by preparing an ancillary control in $|+\rangle$, applying controlled $S_g$, applying a Hadamard to the control and measuring it, with outcome $1$ designated good. These implementations and register initialization have their actual declared costs.

By exact rational comparisons compute the least power of two $M$ satisfying $M^2p_0\ge4$, and the least positive integer $R$ satisfying $(3/4)^R\le\beta$. Set $b=\log_2M$. More general exact parameter representations are allowed only when they support these finite comparisons.

For trials $1,\ldots,R$, carry out the following instructions, stopping at the first return.

1. Prepare $U|0\rangle$ on a fresh register and perform the good/bad instrument. On a good outcome, return that register. On a bad outcome, discard it.
2. Draw exactly $b$ fresh independent unbiased random bits, interpret them as an integer $j\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$, and prepare $U|0\rangle$ on a fresh register. Apply exactly $j$ iterates $Q=-US_0U^\dagger S_g$ of [[alg-qa-12-amplitude-amplification]], then perform the good/bad instrument. On a good outcome, return that register. On a bad outcome, discard it and proceed to the next trial.

If all $R$ trials fail, return an explicit failure symbol. Preparations, bits and instruments are fresh between attempts. A classical-output specialization may additionally measure and verify the returned output, charging this work separately; it does not replace the good/bad projective instrument when a conditional quantum state is requested.

Let $A,\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},a,|G\rangle,|B\rangle$ be as in [[def-qa-12-prepared-success-subspace]], with $0<a<1$, and let $\theta\in(0,\pi/2)$ be the unique angle satisfying $\sin^2\theta=a$. For
$
Q:=-A S_0 A^\dagger S_{\mathrm{good}},
$
the subspace $\operatorname{span}\{|B\rangle,|G\rangle\}$ is invariant. In the ordered orthonormal basis $(|B\rangle,|G\rangle)$, the restriction of $Q$ is
$
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos(2\theta)&-\sin(2\theta)\\
\sin(2\theta)&\cos(2\theta)
\end{pmatrix}.
$
For $a=0$ the prepared vector spans an invariant bad line and $Q|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle$; for $a=1$ it spans an invariant good line and $Q|\psi\rangle=-|\psi\rangle$.

Let $a\in[0,1]$ be the initial success weight and let $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ be the unique angle satisfying $\sin^2\theta=a$. After exactly $k\ge0$ standard amplitude-amplification iterates, the probability of the good outcome of $\{\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},I-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\}$ is
$
\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).
$
The endpoints $a=0$ and $a=1$ are included by direct evaluation, without normalizing a zero component.

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite projective measurement on $H$. Then $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ for every $a$, and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1$.

Let $\rho$ be a density operator and $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ a finite projective measurement on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$. If $p_a>0$, then

$$\rho_a:=\frac{P_a\rho P_a}{p_a}$$

is a density operator whose image $\operatorname{im}(\rho_a):=\{\rho_a x:x\in H\}$ is contained in $\operatorname{im}(P_a)$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). This statement assigns a conditional state only on positive-probability branches.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

One standard iterate expands as
$
Q=-A(I-2|0\rangle\langle0|)A^\dagger(I-2\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}).
$
It therefore uses one good-subspace phase operation, one zero-input phase operation, one forward $A$, and one inverse $A^\dagger$. The initial preparation adds one further forward $A$; optional final verification is separate. A direct reflection about the prepared state is the composite $A S_0 A^\dagger$, not a free primitive unless that separate access is explicitly supplied. Query calls, gates, state preparation, controlled access, and classical costs remain distinct.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, $w(C)$ its total number of wires, and $a_{\rm clean}(C),a_{\rm dirty}(C)$ the numbers of wires that satisfy the exact clean and dirty ancilla contracts of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. Auxiliary wires that satisfy neither contract are still counted in $w(C)$ and are not silently included in either ancilla count ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

On every positive-probability good branch its projection is a scalar multiple of $|g\rangle$, so [F3] gives exactly $|g\rangle\langle g|$. Direct attempts give the same conditional state. If $p=1$, every direct attempt succeeds and returns this state; no zero-probability component is normalized. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

For $0<p<1$, sine addition in [F4] gives $\sin((4j+4)\theta)-\sin(4j\theta)=2\cos((4j+2)\theta)\sin(2\theta)$. Summing over $j=0,\ldots,M-1$ and using $\sin(2\theta)>0$ gives $\sum_j\cos((4j+2)\theta)=\sin(4M\theta)/(2\sin(2\theta))$. Thus the mean success probability of the uniform-index attempt is $a_M=1/2-\sin(4M\theta)/(4M\sin(2\theta))\ge1/2-1/(4M\sin(2\theta))\ge1/2-1/(2M\sin(2\theta))$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

If $0<p<3/4$, then $\sin(2\theta)=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\ge\sqrt p\ge\sqrt{p_0}$. Since $M\ge2/\sqrt{p_0}$, step 1.2 implies $a_M\ge1/4$. The whole trial succeeds with probability $p+(1-p)a_M\ge a_M\ge1/4$. Conditional on any preceding failures, freshness leaves the next trial's success probability at least $1/4$. Finite induction bounds total failure by $(3/4)^R\le\beta$. Every successful branch returns the state of step 1.1; summing its scalar branch weights and dividing by total success probability therefore gives the same density operator, even after forgetting the index, stopping trial and earlier failure outcomes. A trial has at most two preparations and $M-1$ iterates. By [F5], it uses at most $M+1$ forward calls, $M-1$ inverse calls, $M-1$ zero reflections and $M-1$ iterate good reflections. Each of at most two instruments adds one controlled good reflection: on a vector $v$, the control construction has joint state $|0\rangle\otimes(I-P)v+|1\rangle\otimes Pv$ immediately before measurement, which is exactly the required instrument. Thus the displayed per-trial caps hold, and only the second attempt draws $\log_2M$ random bits. [given, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

Minimality of the power of two $M$ gives $2/\sqrt{p_0}\le M<4/\sqrt{p_0}$. Also $R\le1+\ln(1/\beta)/\ln(4/3)$, by applying [F6] to $(3/4)^R\le\beta$ and the minimal positive integer choice. Multiplying the finite per-trial counts by $R$ proves the call and randomness caps and their asymptotic bounds. [given, F1, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

For $-1<y<1$,

$$(\arcsin y)'=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-y^2}},\qquad(\arccos y)'=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

$$C_{\rm cut}(x)=1+\frac{S((x-t)/a_0)-S((x+t)/a_0)}2,\qquad p(x)=\frac{P(x)C_{\rm cut}(x)}{1+e/10}.$$

On a successful certificate, call [[alg-qa-23-qsp-phase-synthesis]] with the checked real odd polynomial $p$ and its degree. Retain its complementary-polynomial and phase certificates and separately record every arithmetic, root, angle, precision, gate, and compiler cost. No exact phase rotation or finite-basis compiler is free.

**Execution.** Execute the QA24 odd QSVT sequence on the adjoint projected-unitary encoding of $\bar A$, with left and right projectors swapped, using the generated phase list and the separately supplied controlled/inverse access. The ideal supported singular-value multiplier is $p(\sigma/\alpha)$; the intended target is $(\delta/2)\bar A^+|b\rangle=(\gamma/2)A^+|b\rangle$. Apply the declared success projector and return its conditional state only on a positive-probability success branch. The scalar polynomial, block-encoding, phase-synthesis, and circuit-implementation errors are separate terms in the supplied error budget.

An optional certified-input branch accepts finite polynomial, phase, and reciprocal-certificate lists; it verifies their parity, interval, identity, and Bernstein checks before execution and returns `INVALID` if a check fails. The Fourier table, coefficient-generation and common-normalization instructions below are the complete original alternate mode. Their generic table/preparation costs remain charged. The complexity guarantee uses `efficient-qsvt`; no such guarantee is inferred for an arbitrary supplied Fourier SELECT circuit or generic coefficient table.

Set $n=m+1$, $\phi_j=2^{-j}$ and $\alpha_{\max}=2/\phi_m$. Supply/construct the actual QA25 sparse block encoding of $A/d$, with every inverse/control form used and its precision/cost. For each stage generate the OP1A polynomial from [[alg-qa-27-qsvt-pseudoinverse]] with gap $\delta_j=\phi_j/d$ and error $e_j\le\min(\delta_j/2,\eta_I/8)$; this invokes its scalar generation instructions only, rather than assuming the stage input has a global gap $\phi_j$. Execute the QA24 real odd QSVT circuit on the adjoint encoding, with its actual real-part-extraction control and zero-workspace success projector. On the spectral subspace $|\lambda|\ge\phi_j$ its target compression is $(\phi_j/2)A^{-1}$, while elsewhere it is simply the declared bounded circuit. Compute a success flag for the whole zero-workspace projector, and dilute its successful component by a separately supplied/constructed flag rotation of amplitude $\phi_m/\phi_j$. This gives the common target $A^{-1}/\alpha_{\max}$; no unspecified PREPARE or SELECT operation occurs in this mode.

In this mode choose the least admissible dyadic QPE scales and least admissible odd repetition counts, and construct the corresponding simulator circuits at their declared precision. Use $\eta_I\le e_*/(4096m\alpha_{\max})$, phase-test amplitude error $\zeta\le\min(e_*/(4096m\alpha_{\max}),1/(4096m\kappa^2))$, and total clean simulation/hybrid error $\eta_S$ bounded by the same minimum. Allocate polynomial, QA23 phase-generation and circuit errors so the actual diluted inverse compression error is at most $\eta_I$. In particular every input-block error obeys $4D_j\sqrt{\epsilon_{{\rm BE},j}}\le\eta_I/8$, where $D_j$ is the actual generated degree; sum all implemented phase/flag/projector errors within the remaining budget. The QA25 small-time-aware simulator is invoked only through its clean-input isometry contract, with an initially clean embedding and the controlled/inverse clean-subspace hybrid of [[lem-qa-25-clean-subspace-unitary-hybrid]]. Within repeated calls and reversal, retain the actual work coherently; only the ideal comparison trajectory has clean work, and actual approximate work is not reset or discarded. Numerical accuracy, all signal/query/gate counts, coefficient/phase generation and arithmetic bit implementation are separate input cost coordinates. The QA23 efficient numerical arithmetic mode grants its stated ideal exact-algebraic operation count only.

**Registers and stopping semantics.** Put $m=\lceil\log_2\kappa\rceil+1$. Use clock bits $C_1,\ldots,C_m$, success bit $F$, system register $I$, separate phase workspaces $P_j$, and coefficient workspace $Q$. Once a clock bit first records a stopped branch, every later stage is controlled on all earlier clock bits being zero. All clock, outcome, and step branches are orthogonal; there are no intermediate measurements in a branch later inverted.

**Finite Fourier inverse (`fourier-table` mode).** For each requested $\phi\in(0,1]$ and error $e_0>0$, `GenerateInverse(φ,e₀)` chooses rational $Y,Z>0$ by increasing integer squares until
$$e^{-\phi^2Y^2/2}/\phi\le e_0/8,\qquad 2Y e^{-Z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\le e_0/8.$$
Set $L_y=Z^2$, $L_z=1+Z^2+YZ$, and choose positive dyadic $\Delta_y,\Delta_z$ with $2YZ(L_y\Delta_y+L_z\Delta_z)/\sqrt{2\pi}\le e_0/8$. Increase $Y,Z$ to multiples of those steps and recheck. For $j=0,\ldots,J-1$, $J=Y/\Delta_y$, and $k=-K,\ldots,K-1$, $K=Z/\Delta_z$, use $y_j=j\Delta_y$, $z_k=k\Delta_z$, and
$$c_{jk}=i\Delta_y\Delta_z z_k e^{-z_k^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$$
for the controlled simulator $e^{-iAy_jz_k}$. Round coefficients with total absolute error at most $e_0/8$, take the rational upper bound $\alpha_\phi=\max(1,\operatorname{upper}(\sum|c_{jk}|))$, pad with cancelling identity terms if needed, and prepare the coefficient table with [[alg-qc-state-preparation]]. A supplied SELECT applies the indicated controlled simulations; PREPARE, SELECT, their inverses, and their costs are explicit. The analytic identity being discretized is
$$\frac1x=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty\!dy\int_{\mathbb R} z e^{-z^2/2}e^{-ixyz}\,dz\quad(|x|\ge\phi).$$
The coefficient PREPARE/SELECT block is the conditional identity proved in [[lem-qa-27-lcu-projected-block-identity]]. The chosen cutoffs and finite coefficients do not by themselves certify the approximation or its gate/bit cost.

For each $\phi_j$, `GPE(φ_j,ζ)` uses a dyadic phase scale at least $64\pi/\phi_j$, an odd number $r\ge8\ln(1/\zeta^2)+8$ of coherent QPE repetitions on the same eigencomponent, and reversible majority comparison of the unwrapped phase magnitude with $3\phi_j/2$. Threshold equality selects the large branch. The promise cases are $|\lambda|\le\phi_j$ and $|\lambda|\ge2\phi_j$; the transition band is unconstrained. Retain all phase work in $P_j$ and make no intermediate measurement.

At stage $j$, conditional on the active prefix $C_1=\cdots=C_{j-1}=0$, run GPE into $C_j,P_j$. On the same prefix and $C_j=1$, execute the common-normalized inverse circuit of the selected mode on $F,Q,I$; otherwise leave the branch unchanged. Let $A_j$ be this stage list, $A=A_m\cdots A_1$, and let $A'_j$ replace its inverse call by a flip of $F$, with $A'=A'_m\cdots A'_1$. The inverse lists are literal reversal with the corresponding inverse calls.

**Terminal bad branch (both modes).** Add a clean terminal bit $T$. After the last GPE/inverse stage, coherently set $T=1$ on the branch with all clock bits zero and leave its success flag zero. This branch is stopped and bad at the final stopping time; it is no longer unfinished. Append the same terminal-bit computation to $A'$ and reverse it inside $(A')^\dagger$. Thus all branches stop by $t_m$, including phase-test failures; the last stopping subspace is the orthogonal union of the ordinary last-stage stop and this terminal-bad branch. Internal good-or-unfinished tests include $T=0$, while the final target is only $F=1$.

**Finite variable-time amplification wrapper (both modes).** Pad cumulative stage counts to increasing dyadic stopping times, preserving stopped branches. Each interval budget includes the supplied input/selected reflections, controlled/inverse list implementations and reversible clock predicates; their costs remain explicit. Form the first sampler by preparing $B|0\rangle$ and running the first interval. Later $B_i$ runs the prior amplified list and the original continuation on unfinished branches only. The initial reflection is about the all-zero state before $B$; $A'$ contains the eigenvalue stages and does not undo $B$.

Let $n=m+1$, $c=1/100$ and $p_{\min}=1/(256n\alpha_{\max}^2)$. The efficient-QSVT mode selects its `efficient-grid` rounding branch; the Fourier-table mode retains its declared rounding branch. This is an arbitrary-sampler estimate, not a Boolean marked-count estimate. Every controlled sampler/inverse and reflection is supplied or built gatewise from an explicit circuit and charged; missing access returns `INVALID_ACCESS`. All estimator registers are fresh construction data, discarded before fresh production execution. A returned estimate $\widehat q_i=0$ gives `ESTIMATION_FAIL`. If $\widehat q_i>1/(9n)$, use $V_i=B_i$. Otherwise choose the least nonnegative integer $k$ with $(2k+1)^2\widehat q_i\ge1/(9n)$, within $k\le\lceil1/\sqrt{p_{\min}}\rceil$; exact rational comparisons or integer binary search implement this selection. A missing crossing gives `ESTIMATION_FAIL`. Execute exactly $k$ ordinary iterates with this sampler and projector. The inequality $(2k+1)^2\widehat q_i\le1/n$ concerns the estimate; no identical actual-success upper bound is assumed.

At the final interval apply [[alg-qa-27-capped-lower-bound-amplification]] to the selected sampler with lower bound $1/(18n)$ and failure $\rho/4$. Copy/measure a separate success record before applying $(A')^\dagger$ to erase internal phase/clock/flag work on the successful branch. In `efficient-qsvt` mode also apply the supplied/constructed all-zero-work projective instrument after this uncompute, return the system only if every work/clock/internal-flag register is zero, and set the external herald to failure otherwise. This makes the conditional returned system state pure; its work-check error/failure is budgeted with $e_*$. The instrument and its controlled-zero reflection/cost are included in $H$. Return the system and external heralding record; a failed branch returns `FAIL`.

For each chosen quantum resource coordinate, construct an integer $H\ge1$ from the actual original-stage, controlled/inverse, selected/input-reflection, dilution and predicate lists, so their interval cost is at most $H2^{j-1}$; enlarge $H$ to include all actually needed gatewise-control depths. For gate coordinates also include the uniform upper bound for the finite estimator's QFT, efficient-grid rounding, rational medians and loop/predicate overhead over every allowed scale through its declared cap; these scales are a finite explicit function of $p_{\min},c,\rho$. Since each sampler-list cost is at least one, this common per-call polynomial-logarithmic factor absorbs that ordinary overhead without treating it as an oracle call. Pad cumulative original stage times to $t_j=H2^j$. Let $r$ be the actual median repetition count of the shared estimator, using its floor and confidence. In `efficient-qsvt` mode impose the additional total primitive-cost cap
$$K=\left\lceil2^{30}(r/c)H\alpha_{\max}n^4\right\rceil.$$
Count construction estimation, list invocations, production, inverse/control/reflection calls and final amplification against this cap and return `RESOURCE_TIMEOUT` before exceeding it. Each coordinate uses its actual $H$ and corresponding cap. Classical coefficient/phase construction, exact algebraic comparisons, output rounding, compiler construction and arithmetic bit work keep their own charged coordinates. The original Fourier mode retains its original declared construction/estimation caps; its distinct table and SELECT costs are not hidden by the efficient-mode quantum cap.

A finite coherent variable-time algorithm has a finite family of stopping times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T_{\max}$, a designated output space, and a finite clock/step register. A run is **unfinished** at stage $j$ if it has not entered a stopping subspace by $t_j$; otherwise it is **stopped**. The stopping subspaces are pairwise orthogonal, and the output register labels each stopped branch as **good** or **bad**. Every later stage is controlled on the unfinished projector, so a stopped branch is not advanced. The input specifies each stage unitary, its inverse and every controlled form used, and the gate/query cost for each.

For a normalized input state, let $p_i$ be the Born probability mass in the subspace that first stops at $t_i$. The masses satisfy $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1$. Define the root-mean-square stopping time
$$T_{\rm av}:=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i t_i^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Let $p_{\rm succ}$ be the total Born probability of the good-output subspace. When $p_{\rm succ}>0$, the good output means the normalized conditional state of the declared good projector; it is defined only on that positive-probability branch. The mean stopping time $\sum_i p_i t_i$ is a different quantity and is not substituted for $T_{\rm av}$.

A measured adaptive procedure qualifies only if it has a finite coherent implementation with the same stopped/unfinished branch semantics and the required inverse/coherent access. Measurement records used to choose a circuit may be classical construction data; no intermediate measurement is inserted into a branch whose later inverse must erase that record. All stopping times, branch probabilities, reflections, inverses, controlled calls, and state preparation remain explicit resource inputs. Complexity statements use an actual normalized primitive-operation coordinate: positive counts are at least one, and the declared interval budgets include the preparation, controlled/inverse and input/selected-reflection operations used in the construction. Other weighted time coordinates may be recorded, but arbitrary uncharged subunit weights do not inherit logarithmic operation-count bounds.

A supplied-probability production regime must specify finite probability/schedule certificates rather than infer them from black-box unitary access. For each dyadic interval it supplies the odd amplification multiplier and certificates relating the actual original good-or-unfinished mass $s_j$, prior selected mass $r_{j-1}$, next mass $q_j=r_{j-1}s_j/s_{j-1}$ and amplified mass $r_j$ to the numerical inequalities required by its theorem; it also supplies a rational constant-factor lower enclosure for the final selected mass. Data may use exact rational/algebraic representations, certified rational enclosures with the stated valid inequalities, or a separately declared exact-real representation/comparison resource. The finite construction and verification cost $C_{\rm build}$ includes every oracle call used to acquire or certify probability information, as well as classical arithmetic, list generation and output costs. No zero-query method obtaining these data is assumed. A uniform regime without those certificates must instead state its supplied probability floor, confidence and complete estimation/production costs. Branch probabilities defined above remain valid analysis quantities even when they are unknown to the implementation.

Let $a\in[0,1]$ be the initial success weight and let $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ be the unique angle satisfying $\sin^2\theta=a$. After exactly $k\ge0$ standard amplitude-amplification iterates, the probability of the good outcome of $\{\Pi_{\mathrm{good}},I-\Pi_{\mathrm{good}}\}$ is
$
\sin^2((2k+1)\theta).
$
The endpoints $a=0$ and $a=1$ are included by direct evaluation, without normalizing a zero component.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer. Let a coherent sampler have success weight $q>0$, and suppose an estimate $\widehat q>0$ satisfies $|\widehat q-q|\le q/100$ and $\widehat q\le1/(9n)$. Choose the least integer $k\ge0$ such that $(2k+1)^2\widehat q\ge1/(9n)$, and put $d=2k+1$, $x=d^2\widehat q$, $y=d^2q$. Applying $k$ standard iterates of [[alg-qa-12-amplitude-amplification]] gives success weight $r$ satisfying
$$\frac1{9n}\le x\le\frac1n,\qquad \frac{100}{101}x\le y\le\frac{100}{99}x,\qquad y\left(1-\frac2{5n}\right)\le r\le y.$$
In particular $1/(16n)\le r\le\min\{1,100/(99n)\}$, and the positive-probability conditional good state is unchanged. The total number of sampler/inverse calls in this fixed amplification is exactly $d$, charging reflections separately.

For any $s\le n$ such amplifications, indexed by $i$, with the same parameter $n$, their multiplicative losses obey
$$\prod_{i=1}^s\frac{r_i}{d_i^2q_i}\ge\frac35,\qquad \prod_{i=1}^s d_i\le\sqrt{\frac53}\prod_{i=1}^s\sqrt{\frac{r_i}{q_i}}.$$

For every promised input of [[alg-qa-relative-probability-estimation]], the procedure terminates. If $p=0$, it returns $\widehat p=0$ with certainty. If $p>0$, then
$$\Pr\{|\widehat p-p|\le cp\}\ge1-\beta.$$

Let $C$ count all invocations of the declared sampler and inverse capabilities: each controlled $A$, controlled $A^*$, and initial ordinary $A$ preparation is counted once in this total, while their individual resource coordinates remain distinct. Put $p_*=\max\{p,p_{\min}\}$, and let $L,r,M_L$ be the algorithm's finite parameters. Then
$$\mathbb E C=O\!\left(\frac{r}{c\sqrt{p_*}}\right),\qquad r=O\!\left(1+\log\frac{L+2}{\beta}\right),\qquad L=O\!\left(1+\log\frac1{p_{\min}}\right).$$
Every execution satisfies the charged cap
$$C<\frac{65rM_L}{c}<\frac{4160r}{c\sqrt{p_{\min}}}.$$
With probability at least $1-\beta$, both $|\widehat p-p|\le cp$ and $C<4160r/(c\sqrt{p_*})$ hold; when $p=0$, both hold deterministically. Thus the expected sampler-and-inverse count is
$$O\!\left(\frac{1+\log((2+\log(1/p_{\min}))/\beta)}{c\sqrt{\max\{p,p_{\min}\}}}\right).$$

These bounds require the algorithm's explicit controlled-access contract. They do not identify a controlled black-box call with an ordinary uncontrolled black-box call. Controlled reflections, control phases, QFT and other ordinary gates, measurements, and classical postprocessing retain separate charged costs. In the retained `exact-cyclotomic` mode, rounding uses finitely many exact algebraic comparisons and produces a rational with $O(\log N)$ bits in each of numerator and denominator at a final scale $N$; no polynomial or polylogarithmic classical-bit bound is asserted. The optional `efficient-grid` mode instead has the helper's uniform polynomial-in-$\log M$ rounding gates, work and generation, while preserving every probability/query bound. Estimation measures only its own construction workspaces, so a subsequent fresh sampler execution, conditional on the returned classical transcript, retains that sampler's prescribed output state and conditional good state.

Under the inputs and promise of [[alg-qa-27-capped-lower-bound-amplification]], that finite procedure succeeds with probability at least $1-\beta$. Conditional on success, its returned register has exactly the density operator $|g\rangle\langle g|$, where $|g\rangle=PU|0\rangle/\sqrt p$. This includes all output and workspace registers of the original conditional good state.

Its deterministic caps are $2RM$ total calls to $U,U^\dagger$, $R(M-1)$ zero-input reflections and $R(M+1)$ good reflections, including the controlled good-reflection calls implementing at most two instruments per trial. It uses at most $R\log_2M$ unbiased random bits. Consequently its primitive-call cap is $O(p_0^{-1/2}(1+\ln(1/\beta)))$, or $O(p_0^{-1/2}\ln(1/\beta))$ when $\beta\le1/2$. Query calls, gates, initialization, instruments, control variants and classical preprocessing are separately charged.

derivations.claim: Group the original operation-count execution into dyadic deadlines, assigning each stopped branch the first deadline after its original stopping count. All counts are positive integers in the declared coordinate. Treat an original stage as indivisible: group all stages ending by each deadline and use twice that deadline as its padded cumulative budget. The interval then covers every grouped whole-stage call. This changes maximum and RMS counts by at most four and leaves stopped branches untouched. There are at most $n$ intervals with increments $\Delta_j$ summing to at most $4T_{\max}$. Their input/selected-reflection and preparation/control budgets are included, rather than treated as free additional operations. We retain this factor in the numerical constants below. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

Let $s_j$ be the original probability of being already good or still unfinished at deadline $j$, with $s_{-1}=1$. It decreases, is at least $p>0$, and has final value $p$. Construct $B_j$ by running the preceding amplified list and continuing the original algorithm only on unfinished branches. Inductively its selected component is proportional to the original selected component, with probability $q_j=r_{j-1}s_j/s_{j-1}$; initially $r_{-1}=1$. Amplify by the chosen odd multiplier. By [F2] this preserves the conditional selected state, and at the last deadline that state is the exact original conditional good state. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Let $v_j$ be the production-list cost and $d_j$ its amplification multiplier. Then $v_j\le d_j(v_{j-1}+\Delta_j)$, with $v_{-1}=0$. The supplied-regime certificate or [F3] gives $d_j\le\sqrt{r_j/q_j}(1-2/(5n))^{-1/2}$ on amplified intervals, with no loss on unamplified intervals. Expand the recurrence. For each summand,
$$\prod_{\ell=j}^{h}\sqrt{r_\ell/q_\ell}=\sqrt{\frac{r_hs_{j-1}}{r_{j-1}p}}.$$
The total loss is at most $\sqrt{5/3}$, and $r_{j-1}\ge1/(16n)$ (with initial value one), so
$$v_h\le6\sqrt{nr_h/p}\sum_j\Delta_j\sqrt{s_{j-1}}.$$
The same bound holds for every prefix with its corresponding $r_i,s_i$. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

Write $u_{j-1}$ for original unfinished mass at the preceding deadline. Since $s_{j-1}\le p+u_{j-1}$ and $\Delta_j\sqrt{u_{j-1}}\le2T_{\rm av}$ by the dyadic stopping convention (also at the first interval, because stopping counts are at least one),
$$S:=\sum_j\Delta_j\sqrt{s_{j-1}}\le4(T_{\max}\sqrt p+nT_{\rm av}).$$
In the supplied-data regime apply [F5] at lower bound $\ell\ge r_h/2$ and constant failure $1/2$. Its $O(r_h^{-1/2})$ factor cancels $\sqrt{r_h}$ in step 2.1, proving production cost $O(T_{\max}\sqrt n+(T_{\rm av}/\sqrt p)n^{3/2})$. Substitute $n=O(\ln L_T)$ and add the actual $C_{\rm build}$, including its probability-acquisition oracle calls. Independent repetitions give the stated confidence. No construction-cost bound follows solely from existence of true-probability-selected multipliers. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

In the uniform regime use [F4] with $c=1/100$, floor $q_{\min}=p_0/(64n)$ and failure $\beta=\rho/(16n)$ at each of at most $n$ intervals. All estimation workspaces are fresh construction data, discarded before production. On the estimator-good event, a returned $\widehat q>1/(9n)$ uses $d=1$ and actual $r=q>(100/101)/(9n)>1/(16n)$, with loss one. Otherwise choose the least odd $d$ with $d^2\widehat q\ge1/(9n)$; search only through $k\le\lceil1/\sqrt{q_{\min}}\rceil$ and return failure if no crossing is found. [F3] gives the same surviving floor and loss bound in this case. Inductively $q_j\ge p/(16n)\ge p_0/(16n)>q_{\min}$, so every estimator promise is met on this joint event; a zero estimate or exhausted search is then impossible. The actual upper bound $r\le1/n$ is neither claimed nor used. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

The prefix version of step 2.1 and $r_{j-1}\ge1/(16n)$ give the next sampler cost $b_i$ the bound $b_i/\sqrt{q_i}\le10\sqrt nS/\sqrt p$. Use step 2.2 and [F4] to charge every estimation call. Summing at most $n$ stages gives at most $2^{18}(r/c)(n^{3/2}T_{\max}+n^{5/2}T_{\rm av}/\sqrt p)$ with slack for dyadic padding. Final production has $v_h\le6\sqrt nS/\sqrt p$. Apply [F5] with floor $1/(18n)$ and failure $\rho/4$: its range is $M<17\sqrt n$, and its trial count $R$ is at most $32r$. Thus its complete additional cost fits within $2^{20}(r/c)n^{5/2}(T_{\max}+T_{\rm av}/\sqrt p)$, again with slack for the already charged reflection/interval overhead. This proves the stated joint-event bound and includes the quantum cost of acquiring probability data. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

The computable integer $P_0$ satisfies $P_0\ge1/\sqrt{p_0}$ and $P_0<2/\sqrt{p_0}$. Since $T_{\rm av}\le T_{\max}$ and $p\ge p_0$, the joint-event cost in step 3.2 is below $K$. Count all construction, production, inverse/control/reflection stage calls and final amplification against $K$, stopping before an excess. The resource timeout therefore never occurs on the joint estimator-good event. Its complement has probability at most $n\beta\le\rho/16$ by [F4] and the union bound. Conditional on the good construction event, final capped amplification fails with probability at most $\rho/4$. Total failure is at most $5\rho/16<\rho$. Every heralded good branch has the same conditional original state by step 1.2, even after averaging the classical construction transcript. The procedure is finite on every branch by its explicit caps. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎
